name: 99designs
tagline: Marketplace where you run a design contest or hire a freelance designer, and pick from the submitted concepts.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: 99designs is not software you are paying for, it is access to a pool of thousands of designers who will actually show up and compete for your brief. The site itself is a brief form, a submission gallery, a messaging thread, and escrow, all of which an agent can clone in an afternoon. What it cannot clone is the part where fifty humans deliver logo concepts by Thursday. You can replace the workflow but not the labor, and the labor is the product. If what you actually want is concepts rather than humans, an AI image pipeline is a different product, not a cheaper 99designs.
coreLoopDIY: A local brief builder that turns your answers into a structured design brief, fans it out to an image model for several concept directions, and stores the variants in a comparable gallery with notes.
requirements: An image generation API key in .env
Node and a local SQLite file
Willingness to accept AI concepts instead of human designers
whatYouLose: Actual human designers with taste, typography skill, and the ability to interpret a vague brief
Contest volume: dozens of genuinely different directions from different heads
Vector source files, print-ready formats, and brand guideline packages
Copyright transfer, escrow, and someone to chase if the work is plagiarized
Revision rounds with a person who remembers what you said last time
moatNotes: Two-sided liquidity plus a reputation and ratings graph built over a decade. The buyer shows up because the designers are there, and vice versa.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because hiring one designer is a bet and a contest is a hedge. For a few hundred dollars you get a spread of directions from people who do this all day, you keep the one you like, and the rights transfer cleanly. Solo founders pay for that specifically to avoid spending three weeks nudging an image model toward something that still looks like a 2023 AI logo. The escrow and the dispute process also mean you are not wiring money to a stranger and hoping.
notes: The contest UI is a weekend build; the designers are not. The moat is marketplace liquidity: a standing pool of thousands of designers who reliably answer a brief within days.
prompt:
Build a local design concept workbench called BriefBench. It is NOT a marketplace. It is a single-user tool for turning a vague idea into a structured brief and a gallery of AI-generated concept directions I can compare.

Stack, no alternatives: Next.js with the app router, TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite via better-sqlite3. Run with npm run dev on localhost. No auth, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Features:
1. Brief builder: a multi-step form capturing project type (logo, wordmark, social kit, packaging), business name, what the business does in one sentence, target audience, three adjectives for the vibe, three brands to emulate, colors to use, colors to avoid, and hard constraints. Save each brief as a record.
2. Brief compiler: render the saved answers into a clean markdown brief, viewable and copyable, plus a derived image prompt for each of exactly five named directions: Minimal Geometric, Literal Icon, Typographic Only, Retro Badge, Abstract Mark.
3. Concept generation: a server route that calls an image generation API using IMAGE_API_KEY from .env, three images per direction, stored under /public/concepts and referenced in SQLite. Show a spinner, handle failures per-image without killing the batch.
4. Gallery: grid grouped by direction, click to enlarge, star favorites, per-image notes field, and a filter for starred only.
5. Round two: pick one image, write a revision note, regenerate three variants of that direction with the note appended to the prompt. Keep lineage so I can see parent and children.
6. Export: a button that writes a folder with the markdown brief, the starred images, and a notes.md of every comment.

Explicitly out of scope: designer profiles, bidding, messaging, payments, escrow, vector output, SVG tracing, print formats.

Include a seeded example brief, a .env.example with IMAGE_API_KEY, and a README that says plainly in the first paragraph that this produces raster concept directions for exploration only, not finished brand assets, and that someone will still need to redraw the winner in vector.
